query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In multi‐phase eutectic high-entropy alloys with chemically distinct lamellae, accelerated coupled degradation under elevated temperature arises from differential oxidation kinetics. The more rapidly oxidizing phase (e.g., Al-rich) forms a less protective oxide that, when juxtaposed with a slowly oxidizing phase (e.g., Cr-rich), creates a galvanic couple. Under mechanical wear, the non-protective oxide undergoes spallation, exposing fresh reactive surfaces that further accentuate localized corrosion. This cyclical process—combining differential oxide formation, galvanic corrosion at the phase interfaces, and wear-induced removal of the protective layers—leads to significantly enhanced total material degradation relative to conditions where oxidation is more uniform.
generation.material_initial_state: Multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy composed of chemically distinct lamellae (for example, having Al-rich and Cr-rich phases) in the as-processed state.
generation.intervention: Conduct controlled experiments where samples are subjected to identical high-temperature sliding wear while varying the oxygen partial pressure; one condition will use a high oxygen partial pressure to promote differential oxidation, and the baseline condition will use a low oxygen partial pressure to favor uniform oxidation.
generation.conditions: Elevated temperature (approximately 500–600 °C), identical wear loads applied through reciprocating sliding wear tests, and a corrosive environment that can be tuned in oxygen partial pressure (high oxygen vs. low oxygen conditions).
generation.structural_mediator: The formation of different oxide types at the phase boundaries resulting from inherent differences in oxidation kinetics between the distinct phases.
generation.mechanism: Differential oxidation causes one phase (e.g., the Al-rich lamellae) to rapidly form a nonprotective oxide while the adjacent Cr-rich phase oxidizes more slowly, leading to localized galvanic couples. The resulting oxidized interfaces are more susceptible to mechanical spallation under wear, exposing fresh reactive surfaces and thus perpetuating a vicious cycle of localized corrosion and wear.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under high oxygen partial pressure, the alloy will exhibit a higher total degradation rate compared to the baseline low oxygen condition. Specifically, there will be deeper corrosion pits (due to accelerated galvanic corrosion) and increased wear damage due to the spallation of inadequately protective oxides at the heterogeneous phase boundaries.
generation.baseline: Observations from tests under low oxygen partial pressure, where oxidation is more uniform and less prone to differential oxide formation, thereby reducing the galvanic effect and the associated accelerated coupled degradation.
generation.boundary: Results are expected to hold for the specified elevated temperature range (500–600 °C) and wear testing conditions; deviations outside these parameters may alter oxidation rates and wear behavior.
generation.uncertainty: While the qualitative mechanism is supported by existing evidence on differential oxidation and galvanic corrosion in multi-phase alloys, quantitative predictions of degradation acceleration (e.g., exact rates or thresholds) remain uncertain without further experimental calibration.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare identical samples of the eutectic HEA and divide them into two groups. Subject one group to sliding wear tests at elevated temperature within a high oxygen partial pressure environment and the other group to the same tests under low oxygen partial pressure conditions. Monitor the degradation using cross-sectional microscopy and weight loss measurements over time.
measurements: Wear track depth analysis via microscopy
Surface compositional analysis (e.g., EDX mapping) to track oxide distribution
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if no statistically significant differences are observed in either local corrosion (e.g., pit depth) or wear damage (e.g., track depth, weight loss) between the high oxygen and low oxygen conditions, or if the differential oxidation and galvanic interaction at phase boundaries are not observed via surface analysis.

cited_evidence.text: Furthermore, in the low-frequency range, all tested surfaces were characterized by high impedance above 105 Ω·cm2, indicating that these surfaces have adequate corrosion resistance in a 0.9% NaCl solution, making them suitable for medical applications in this respect. All tested materials behaved almost like an ideal capacitor.SEM-EDS analysis of the surface after the corrosion tests revealed that in the case of the AlCoCrMFeNi equivalent alloy, corrosion occurs due to Cr segregation, where the Cr-depleted grain interiors are predisposed to the formation of corrosion pits, and the Al- and Ni-rich grain interiors are subject to corrosion. Areas rich in Al and Ni form the anode, while areas rich in Cr form the cathode. In the case of HEA with Mo, pits developed at the boundaries of areas enriched in Cr and Mo, leading to galvanic corrosion with an adjacent matrix (rich in Al and Ni).

AbstractIn this study, the wear behaviour of a powder metallurgically produced AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 high-entropy alloy (HEAs) is investigated at elevated temperatures. Spark plasma sintering (SPS) of inert gas atomised feedstock enables the production of dense bulk material. The microstructure evolution and phase formation are analysed. The high cooling rate in the atomisation process results in spherical powder with a microstructure comprising two finely distributed body-centred cubic phases. An additional phase with a complex crystal structure precipitates during SPS processing, while no coarsening of microstructural features occurs. The wear resistance under reciprocating wear conditions increases at elevated temperatures due to the formation of a protective oxide layer under atmospherical conditions. Additionally, the coefficient of friction (COF) slightly decreases with increasing temperature. SPS processing is suitable for the production of HEA bulk material. An increase in the wear resistance at elevated temperature enables high temperature applications of the HEA system AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5.Keywords: high-entropy alloy (HEA), compositionally complex alloy (CCA), spark plasma sinterin

proposals.material_system: Eutectic HEA similar to AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5 produced via SPS (as in PMC7515071)
proposals.intervention: Design a controlled experiment comparing tribocorrosion behavior under two conditions: one with an environment that permits natural oxide formation and spallation, and another under controlled inert gas conditions (minimizing oxide reformation) at the same elevated temperature and wear loads.
proposals.conditions: Elevated temperature (e.g., 500–600 °C), simultaneous sliding wear under reciprocating motion, and a corrosive environment (such as a chloride-containing gas or salt fog) versus an inert atmosphere to suppress oxide dynamics.
proposals.structural_mediator: The dynamic formation and wear-induced spallation of protective oxide layers on the multi-phase interfaces.
proposals.mechanism: Wear action repeatedly removes the initially protective oxide film that forms at high temperature. This exposes fresh, reactive surfaces that accelerate localized corrosion. The corrosive attack subsequently undermines the integrity of the remaining oxide and the alloy’s microstructure, leading to a vicious cycle that rapidly increases degradation via both wear and corrosion.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Compared to the inert baseline, the naturally oxidizing environment will show a higher total degradation: an increased wear depth combined with enhanced corrosion penetration. Individually, the corrosion rate will be elevated due to oxide removal, and wear damage will be exacerbated due to weakened substrate support.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This hypothesis integrates the synergy of wear and corrosion at high temperature through the removal and reformation cycle of protective oxides, offering a single mechanistic explanation for coupled accelerated degradation. The controlled comparison (inert vs. oxidizing atmospheres) directly distinguishes the role of the dynamic oxide film.

proposals.material_system: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with distinct lamellar phases (e.g., a designed eutectic variant of CoCrFeMnNi-based systems)
proposals.intervention: Introduce a pre-thermal treatment to induce differential residual stresses at the eutectic interfaces and compare samples with and without this pre-stressing, then subject both to identical high-temperature wear–corrosion testing.
proposals.conditions: Elevated temperature (e.g., ~500 °C), identical tribocorrosion loads, and a corrosive medium (e.g., simulated high-temperature oxidizing atmosphere with corrosive species), with one set of samples pre-treated for controlled thermal cycling to introduce interface stresses.
proposals.structural_mediator: Weak interphase (eutectic interface) regions where differential thermal expansion and alloying element mismatch promote stress concentration.
proposals.mechanism: The pre-existing residual stress localized at eutectic boundaries, when subjected to simultaneous wear and corrosion, leads to rapid interphase decohesion. This microcrack formation at phase boundaries facilitates increased penetration of corrosive agents and promotes accelerated material removal by wear.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Relative to the baseline alloy (without pre-stress), pre-treated samples will exhibit higher rates of degradation, with particularly evident wear intensity along the eutectic interfaces and deeper corrosion pits. Total degradation increases as the synergistic effects overwhelm the interface bonding.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: By focusing on the integrity of phase boundaries under combined degradation conditions, this proposal links mechanistic interface weakening (caused by thermal residual stress and corrosion) to accelerated coupled degradation. The controlled comparison isolates the role of interfacial residual stresses.

proposals.material_system: Eutectic HEA system in a CoCrFeMnNi family processed by severe plastic deformation (SPD) to obtain a refined nanostructure
proposals.intervention: Compare a fine-grained (SPD-processed) alloy with a conventional coarse-grained counterpart under identical high-temperature wear–corrosion conditions.
proposals.conditions: Testing at elevated temperatures (around 500–600 °C) in a corrosive environment (e.g., a medium containing oxide-forming species) under identical wear loads; controlled variables include processing route and grain size.
proposals.structural_mediator: Enhanced grain boundary density in the SPD-processed alloy, which serves as rapid diffusion paths for oxygen and corrosive species.
proposals.mechanism: In the fine-grained structure, a high density of grain boundaries accelerates localized oxidation along these interfaces. The resulting grain boundary oxides are less protective and more prone to spallation under mechanical sliding, which in turn exposes fresh grain boundaries to corrosion. This synergy between grain boundary oxidation and wear accelerates total degradation.
proposals.predicted_outcome: The SPD-processed fine-grained alloy will exhibit a higher total degradation rate, with both an increased corrosion penetration (due to aggressive grain boundary oxidation) and elevated wear damage (due to brittle oxide removal), compared with the baseline coarse-grained alloy.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This direction pinpoints the role of microstructure (grain size and boundary density) in triggering a single mechanistic cycle where rapid oxidation and subsequent removal under wear conditions accelerate overall degradation.

proposals.material_system: Multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy featuring chemically distinct phases (e.g., an alloy with Al-rich and Cr-rich lamellae)
proposals.intervention: Conduct controlled experiments altering the oxygen partial pressure to selectively modify the oxidation kinetics of the different phases, while subjecting samples to identical wear stress.
proposals.conditions: Elevated temperature (around 500–600 °C) with two environmental conditions: one with high oxygen partial pressure promoting differential oxidation and one with low oxygen partial pressure achieving more uniform oxidation. Concurrent application of identical wear cycles in both conditions.
proposals.structural_mediator: Differential oxide formation at the phase boundaries due to distinct oxidation rates of Al-rich versus Cr-rich regions.
proposals.mechanism: Due to inherent differences in the oxidation kinetics of the constituent phases, a galvanic couple forms when one phase (e.g., Al-rich) oxidizes more rapidly than the adjacent Cr-rich phase. This leads to localized corrosion at the phase interfaces, and when combined with mechanical wear, the junctions experience accelerated material removal. The coupled degradation arises from the synergy between localized galvanic corrosion and enhanced wear at the chemically mismatched boundaries.
proposals.predicted_outcome: Under high oxygen partial pressure, the alloy will show a higher overall degradation rate with pronounced local corrosion pitting and increased wear at the phase boundaries relative to the baseline condition (low oxygen partial pressure), where oxidation is more uniform and less detrimental.
proposals.why_it_addresses_the_question: This approach isolates the effect of differential oxidation kinetics, providing a single mechanistic explanation where galvanic interactions and selective oxide instability drive the accelerated coupled degradation. The controlled oxygen environment provides a clear criterion to falsify the hypothesis if no significant degradation differences are observed.

decision.rationale: Direction D directly targets the multi‐phase nature of the eutectic HEA by proposing that chemically distinct phases (e.g., Al‐rich versus Cr‐rich lamellae) show differential oxidation kinetics. This difference leads to local galvanic cells at phase boundaries that, in combination with mechanical wear (which continually removes the nonprotective oxide), form a self‐reinforcing cycle of localized corrosion and accelerated material removal. This hypothesis best explains the simultaneous enhancement of corrosion and wear degradation and can be cleanly evaluated by altering oxygen partial pressures. The supporting literature (e.g., PMC12525669) indicates that galvanic interactions due to compositional heterogeneity can drive corrosion, making this a compelling single mechanistic explanation.
